title: From Bhag Club to Bombay On Foot: How India's Run Club Boom Is Rewriting the Wellness Playbook
excerpt: Across India's cities, running clubs are replacing bar crawls as the new social ritual — and the movement is resonating with the diaspora seeking community beyond the treadmill.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Run clubs are replacing traditional social gatherings in India's cities.
  • 91% of Gen Z fitness enthusiasts in India engage in multiple workout formats.
  • India has 2.5 million registered runners and over 1,600 annual running events.
  • Running clubs address loneliness, fostering community and social connections.
  • Indian-origin run clubs are emerging globally, connecting diaspora communities.

The most popular social plans in India's metros no longer start at midnight. They start at 6 a.m.

Across Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, and beyond, a new kind of social institution has taken root — the run club. Not the stodgy, competitive racing circles of a decade ago, but vibrant, inclusive communities where the post-run chai matters as much as the pace, and where strangers become friends over shared miles. It is, by many accounts, the most significant shift in Indian wellness culture since yoga studios went mainstream.

The New Third Space

Run clubs have become what sociologists call a "third space" — a gathering point that exists outside the binary of home and work. Groups like Bhag Club in Delhi, Bombay On Foot in Mumbai, Daud Run Club in Bengaluru, and Pudhechala Run Club have turned early mornings into something aspirational.

"Wellness is a happy state of mind, and that happiness is strengthened when communities come together," says Jyotiraditya Thakur, founder of Bhag Club, which now counts 300 to 400 loyal runners. The club's programming goes well beyond training schedules. Park Baddies, a women-only monthly gathering, hosts beach runs, artist collaborations, ice baths, and recovery rituals. The club recently organised an adults' sports day in Mumbai — complete with sack races, lemon-and-spoon relays, and the kind of uninhibited joy rarely seen outside a school playground.

Bombay On Foot, founded by Soham Arora and Tanish Agarwal, pushes the envelope further with DJ-led runs, hydration-focused long routes, and post-run community breakfasts. "People are drawn to community wellness because it solves two problems at once — physical health and loneliness," the founders explain.

The Numbers Back It Up

The data confirms what the 6 a.m. crowds suggest. According to Strava, the fitness tracking app, 2025 saw a 1.5-times increase in club events organised globally, with 39 percent more Gen Z participants than Gen X saying they use fitness to meet like-minded people. In India specifically, the fitness platform Fitpass reports that 91 percent of its Gen Z members — drawn from over 600,000 users — practice at least three different workout formats, and 83 percent visit more than two fitness centres monthly.

India now has 2.5 million registered runners and over 1,600 running events annually. Marathon registrations have soared since the pandemic, with the Tata Mumbai Marathon attracting around 60,000 participants, including over 12,000 who ran the full distance.

"There's a visible shift toward fitness-led, community-based activities," says Nagaraj Adiga, chairman of NEB Sports Entertainment, which organises multiple road races including the Apollo Tyres New Delhi Marathon. "Running clubs, social runs, and weekend challenges have become the new social circles."

More Than Fitness

What makes the movement culturally significant is that it addresses India's growing loneliness epidemic. Global surveys indicate that nearly one in four young adults experience significant loneliness, and India is no exception. As digital interactions proliferate, the run club offers something screens cannot: eye contact, shared exhaustion, collective achievement.

"Stress intensifies in isolation, but it softens in solidarity," observes Dr. Rachna Khanna Singh, Senior Consultant in Mental Wellness at Artemis Hospital Gurgaon. She points to a meta-analysis in *PLOS Medicine* that found individuals with strong social relationships have a 50 percent higher likelihood of survival compared to those with weaker ties.

The phenomenon extends beyond pure running. Pickleball leagues, cycling crews, dance collectives, and curated wellness experiences are all part of the same social wellness boom. In Goa, Solene club offers breathwork ceremonies and mindful movement sessions. In Delhi, Evolve Wellness Club creates women-only spaces combining sound healing, yoga, and meditation.

The Diaspora Connection

For NRIs watching from abroad, India's run club revolution resonates deeply. Indian-origin run clubs have emerged in New York, London, Toronto, and the San Francisco Bay Area, often explicitly modelled on the communal spirit of groups back home. For diaspora communities navigating the isolation that often accompanies immigration, these clubs offer more than cardio — they offer belonging.

"When someone completes their first 5K after believing they couldn't, that matters to us," say the founders of Bombay On Foot. It is a sentiment that translates across borders, time zones, and the particular brand of loneliness that comes with building a life far from where you started.

Global Diaspora Connections

The real luxury of 2026, it turns out, is not feeling better alone. It is feeling better together.

*Sources: Global Spa Online; Strava Year in Sport Report; Fitpass India; Elle India; The Style List India; NEB Sports Entertainment*
